title: In vitro fertilisation (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) | NHS inform
text:
In vitro fertilisation (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)
Not all information on this page will be relevant for everyone. All couples can access NHS fertility services if they meet the
treatment access criteria
. This includes same-sex couples and couples where 1 or both partners are trans or non-binary.
In vitro fertilisation (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) are fertility procedures. They help those with
infertility
issues try to conceive a child.
IVF
IVF involves taking eggs from the ovaries and mixing them with sperm in a laboratory. This creates an embryo. The embryo is then implanted into the woman’s womb (uterus).
ICSI
ICSI is similar to IVF but the sperm is injected into an egg, instead of mixing the sperm and egg together. This is carried out when the sperm is low quality.
IVF and ICSI are not the only options to treat infertility. It’s important that you speak to your GP if you feel you are struggling with infertility.
Further information about infertility
Who needs IVF and ICSI?
Some of the reasons your medical professional may recommend IVF or ICSI include:
Blocked or damaged fallopian tubes
This can prevent eggs from reaching the uterus on their own.
Ovulation disorders
Conditions like
polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
or irregular ovulation might require IVF.
Male infertility
IVF, combined with ICSI can help address issues such as:
low sperm count
poor sperm motility (ability to move)
abnormal sperm shape
Endometriosis
Endometriosis
a long-term (chronic) condition where tissue (similar to the lining of the womb) is found elsewhere in the body.
Genetic disorders
Embryos can be tested for genetic disorders before implantation (
preimplantation genetic testing (PGT
)). This help prevent genetic conditions being passed on.
Unexplained infertility
Sometimes no clear cause of infertility can be identified after thorough investigation.
You may also be recommended IVF or ICSI if you’re:
a same-sex couple
planning on using a surrogacy
What can affect IVF and ICSI success?
There are factors that can affect the success of IVF and ICSI, including:
age — success rates decrease as you get older
egg number— the number of eggs collected may affect the chances of fertilisation
egg and sperm quality — poor-quality eggs or sperm can lower chance of fertilisation
health of the uterus – abnormalities in the uterus, fibroids, or scar tissue can affect implantation
previous pregnancies — previous successful pregnancies can mean improved outcomes
Smoking tobacco, drinking too much alcohol, obesity, and high stress can negatively impact fertility.
Getting started with IVF and ICSI
The process typically involves several steps.
Consultation
A fertility specialist will evaluate your health. They’ll also discuss the best options for you and the process involved.
Ovarian stimulation
Hormones have to be taken to stimulate the ovaries. This helps to produce multiple eggs. The growth of eggs will be monitored using an ultrasound.
Egg retrieval
Once the eggs are mature, you’ll be sedated or given an anaesthetic and the eggs will be collected. This involves a minor surgical procedure using a small needle.
Sperm collection
At the time of egg collection, a sperm sample will also be collected from the male partner. This will either be through ejaculation or, less often, through
surgical sperm retrieval
. If using donor sperm, the sperm will be thawed before fertilisation.
Fertilisation
For IVF, the eggs are mixed with sperm (either from a partner or donor) in a laboratory. For ICSI, a sperm is injected into the egg(s).
Embryo culture and monitoring
Your fertilised eggs (embryos) are monitored to check they grow and divide properly. Embryologists (fertility scientists) assess the quality of the embryos during this time.
Embryo transfer
The best-quality embryo is selected for transfer into your womb (or a surrogates womb). The process uses a thin catheter (tube) to place the embryo into the womb. If you have multiple good-quality embryos, some may be frozen for later use.
Pregnancy test
About 10 to 14 days after the embryo transfer, you’ll take a pregnancy test. A scan will be taken a few weeks later to confirm pregnancy.
If you become pregnant, you’ll be discharged for maternity care.
If you’re not pregnant, you may be invited for a review appointment. If you have frozen embryos, these can be transferred into your womb. If you do not have frozen embryos, you may be eligible for another round of IVF or ICSI.
In some case your fertility specialist may advise you of other treatments.
Treatment on the NHS
Not all patients
will be eligible for NHS treatment
. For example, if you and your partner already have a child together.
